1#main: The laws of grafting trees. In it are 7 seifim. Kilayim of trees are included in what was said, "Your field you shall not sow with kilayim." How so? One who grafts a tree onto a tree—for example, grafted a shoot of apple onto citron or citron onto apple—receives lashes d'oraisa everywhere, both in Eretz Yisrael and in the Diaspora. And likewise one who grafts a vegetable onto a tree or a tree onto a vegetable receives lashes everywhere.
2#main: It is forbidden for an Israelite to allow a non-Jew to graft his tree as kilayim.
3#main: It is permitted to sow seeds and the seed of a tree together; and likewise permitted to mix seeds of trees and sow them together, for you have kilayim in trees only through grafting alone—whether tree with vegetable, vegetable with tree, or vegetable with vegetable that is not its species; and even a wood tree on a food tree or a food tree on a wood tree.
4#main: There is a prohibition of grafting even under the ground—for example, a vine shoot that was layered under the ground: it is forbidden to sow vegetables upon it unless there is three tefachim of earth on top of it; and even if the layering was inside a gourd that dried out, or inside a pipe of earthenware, because it takes root in it and it becomes grafting of vegetable onto tree. And if there was less than this on top, it is forbidden to sow on top of it; but it is permitted to sow at its side. But layering in rock is difficult: even if there is no earth on it but three fingerbreadths, it is permitted to bring seed upon it. When does this apply? When the main vine is not visible; but if it is visible, one must distance six tefachim in every direction and then sow, as one distances from every individual vine that was not layered.
5#main: And specifically in this manner, which is called by the name "tree" before it was layered; but it is permitted to sow next to the tree even though the roots of the vegetables enter within the roots of the tree, since the roots do not have the name "tree." And even regarding layering—specifically in a vine shoot because it is soft and the roots of seeds enter it; but one who layers a branch from another tree—it is permitted to sow on top of it even if there are not three fingerbreadths of earth on it.
6#main: There are among trees some similar to one another in leaves or in fruit, and nevertheless since they are two species, these are kilayim with one another. How so? Apple with quince (meaning: a forest apple species); peach (meaning: persica in the vernacular) with oleaster (meaning: he grafted olives on pomegranate, which are fruit similar to olive, and oleaster comes out from them) with pomegranate—even though they are similar to one another, they are kilayim with one another. But pears (in the vernacular) with crustumenian pears (a species of pears), and quince with medlars (sorbele in the vernacular) are not kilayim with one another. {Rama: And likewise it is permitted to graft one species even black on white and thin on thick, even though it has an accompanying name (Kol Bo and Bach in the name of Orach Chaim). And likewise wood on wood is permitted even if not its species (so it appears from the Tur). Nevertheless, since most of the world does not recognize most species, it is good to be careful with all of them (Beit Yosef in the name of Semak).}
7#main: It is forbidden to maintain what was grafted as kilayim; but the fruit that comes from it is permitted—even for the one who transgressed and grafted it. And it is permitted to take a branch from the grafted tree and plant it elsewhere.
